#10549. AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Big US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

As governments scramble to make AI safer, who gets to write the rules could be just as important as what they say.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more.

First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The company launched the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra.

But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI said Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want.

It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve.

For years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do.

OpenAI says that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here.

Those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments.

Against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview.

But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO. "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of users,” von Thun said. “They’re definitely vulnerable.”

Those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months.

That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a company’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics.

In July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy Loke, an AI governance researcher at King's College London who specialises in China's approach to the technology, questions the timing. "It's very suspicious timing asking for pacing," she told Tom's Hardware Premium, referring to calls for slowing frontier AI development just as Chinese open-weight models are undercutting their American rivals on price.

Loke believes companies genuinely worry about the risks. But she also thinks they're worried about their commercial prospects. "they're calling for pacing because they have some safety concerns, they have some commercial anxiety," she said.

She believes some influential people in American AI have increasingly sought to "paint open models in a very bad light", portraying them as inherently less secure than closed alternatives. Yet the risks of AI systems misbehaving aren't restricted to models developed in China, as OpenAI's own incidents demonstrate.

But open-weight models come with their own risks. Because their underlying parameters can be modified, third parties can create and distribute "abliterated" models, removing the refusal behaviours designed to prevent AI from responding to potentially harmful requests. Many of these models are available on platforms including Hugging Face. “They’re not adding in new behaviour; they’re just removing this refusal behaviour,” said Catherine Flick, professor of ethics and games technology at the University of Staffordshire, in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium. Abliterating models doesn’t make them more capable, Flick said, but it does mean they can answer questions they previously wouldn’t have been willing to. That also means those responses might not have been tested for accuracy or hallucinations.

Those in favour of open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen say that removing those guardrails helps security researchers understand how AI behaves. Flick said that’s plausible, but “I just don’t really buy it,” she said. She reckons that the negative potential outputs outweigh the positive case for abliteration because when they’re publicly available, preventing their misuse becomes tricky. American labs clearly have commercial reasons to criticise open-weight competitors because the latter undercuts their economics, but it also doesn’t mean their concerns about safety aren’t valid, too.

Von Thun fears that could result in precisely the wrong kind of regulation. "I think what we should not be doing is allowing the companies to basically form a safety cartel," he said.

Yet U.S. AI companies benefit from the government's determination to maintain its advantage over China. Von Thun argues the Trump administration has created an environment in which economic power translates into political influence, allowing major technology companies to invoke national security concerns when arguing for policies that may also serve their commercial interests. But that could backfire. "I think completely closing off the market to AI products from other countries, including China, would not be the right approach," von Thun said.

Part of the reason that wouldn’t be the right approach is that the idea that the United States is focused on developing AI responsibly while China isn’t is a fallacy. Just earlier this month, Reuters reported that ByteDance had established a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team, recruiting researchers to investigate safety risks arising from increasingly capable AI systems.

For von Thun, the solution is to prevent either industry or geopolitical competition from determining what safety means. He points to the European Union's AI Act, which establishes obligations for developers of general-purpose AI models classified as posing systemic risks. The obligations require companies to conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures and also to report serious incidents.

The opposition to the EU’s AI Act from American tech companies, U.S. politicians and the general public who grouse about the way it delays access to cutting-edge models for Europe’s 450 million citizens demonstrates that these provisions don't automatically solve the alignment problem. But they at least involve more people in the conversation about what is and isn’t acceptable for AI than just the industry's biggest participants.

Even when AI companies agree to independent oversight, they still want some say over how it works — and their own internal decision-making on what is and isn’t safe differs from that of those outside the company. Loke warns that leading AI companies are experimenting with recursive self-improvement, where models help develop their successors, potentially making it more difficult for humans to understand how decisions are being made. "They’re still attempting more risky methods to train AI that will make the AI harder to control," she said.

Von Thun also believes competition rules and interoperability requirements could help prevent AI companies from locking customers into proprietary ecosystems as their agents become increasingly embedded in everyday workflows.

There are plenty of good reasons to be concerned about alignment, particularly when the models being developed are becoming more capable and more difficult to monitor. But letting the companies responsible for building them determine what constitutes an acceptable risk, and who can compete, brings its own dangers. “I’m not saying we don’t need to worry about safety,” said von Thun, “but we should about letting the companies do it."

Chris Stokel-Walker is a Tom's Hardware contributor who focuses on the tech sector and its impact on our daily lives— online and offline. He is the author of How AI Ate the World, published in 2024, as well as TikTok Boom, YouTubers, and The History of the Internet in Byte-Sized Chunks.

#10548. Mental health’s short-term mindset problem

When I struggled with anorexia as an adolescent, I learned that the traditional healthcare ecosystem had a simplified view of recovery: stabilize vitals and clear the patient out to keep costs down.

Now, as an eating disorder treatment founder and CEO, I spend my days working with collaborative health insurance plans to fix these historical dynamics. Together, we’ve made incredible progress toward value-based care, a system that rewards treatment providers for getting patients better rather than for how often patients see them.

But as the mental health industry works to measure real clinical impact, providers and health plans share the same roadblock: overreliance on immediate, short-term financial ROI.

Because health plans and employers usually operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles, standard financial models naturally hunt for quick wins, like preventing an ER visit within that same year. Behavioral health doesn’t fit into a short-term box.

This isn’t about bad intentions; it’s just how the financial system was built. In practice, though, it leaves out people managing on the outside who still need real support before things get worse.

THE STRUCTURAL CHALLENGE

Real health savings take time. We already spend money upfront to manage conditions like diabetes, because it prevents far more expensive health emergencies years later. Behavioral health needs that same long-term investment.

A major roadblock is that behavioral and physical health costs are tracked in separate silos. On paper, investing in mental health looks like an extra expense, even when it directly drives down physical healthcare costs, like expensive hospital admissions.

I lived this firsthand: I appeared as a “zero-cost” member on claims data until I was hospitalized, leading to months of treatment. Early intervention could have prevented immense suffering and expense, yet data shows nearly 40% of pediatric eating disorder patients first enter the healthcare system under general medical complaints rather than a behavioral health diagnosis. When hospitalization does occur, the median time from diagnosis to admission is under a month.

THE MYTH OF THE “LOW-RISK” MEMBER

The true cost of mental illness isn’t always apparent in claims data. For example, millions of people struggling with things like severe eating disorders, OCD, major depression, and anxiety arrive at work or school every day, meet their daily goals, turn in homework, and maintain a general outward appearance of being well.

Because they aren’t ending up in emergency rooms or generating high costs, they’re viewed as low-cost.

Evaluating mental healthcare strictly on one-year cost savings makes it hard to justify giving high-functioning people the full support they need. On paper, their immediate medical costs look minimal, so why invest in specialized care before something terrible happens?

Under standard short-term budget cycles, care is too often delayed until it becomes a crisis, costing both the person and their health plan much more in the long run.

CO-CREATE THE NEXT PHASE OF VALUE-BASED CARE

Health plans are the indispensable engine of healthcare innovation, and real systemic change happens only when health plans and care providers agree on incentives—something I’ve seen firsthand with some of the partners we work with at Equip. Moving beyond short-term cost containment toward long-term value on investment (VOI) requires new frameworks:

  • Health plan partnerships could look at whether people are regaining their lives—such as staying symptom-free, doing well at work, and feeling good—instead of just counting how many people stayed out of the hospital. 
  • Health insurance plans and employers can work together on long-term contracts, giving treatment the time it needs to pay off in real, cumulative savings.
  • Getting people help early keeps them healthy and stops small problems from turning into bigger ones. The crazy thing is, the current system only rewards fixing things after they break. So when someone actually steps up and chooses to get help, the system sees that as an extra bill instead of a huge win.

Fixing this doesn’t mean ignoring financial reality, but we need to look at the bigger picture together. To fulfill the promise of value-based care, we need models that match the reality of recovery.

Resilience should open doors to care, not close them, and together, we can build a healthcare system that keeps people well before they break.

Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.

#10547. AI is today’s light bulb

In 2004, I set out to do something many in the energy business thought was crazy: digitize the last mile of the electric grid—the wires and meters between the substation and the homes and businesses it serves. My bet was that internet protocol, the common language of the world’s computers, would eventually connect the grid too. Once it did, every meter and sensor could talk to the software running it.

Plenty of smart people told me it would never happen. Utilities, like pipeline, rail, and water operators, plan in decades; they cannot afford to get reliability wrong. So the real work was finding the handful of utility leaders willing to go first.

Two decades later, more than three out of four electric meters in the United States are smart meters, over 128 million of them, according to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

I bring this up because I believe we are at the start of something much bigger now, that reaches beyond the grid to every system the economy runs on. AI is today’s light bulb: It’s what everyone can see. But the revolution is the network underneath it, and most leaders are looking at the wrong part.

EDISON’S REAL INVENTION WAS THE NETWORK

When Thomas Edison switched on his Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan on September 4, 1882, he was selling light. Within a month, 59 customers were using it to light about 400 lamps. By 1884, it served more than 500 customers.

In The Age of Edison, historian Ernest Freeberg shows that what remade American cities wasn’t the light bulb itself but what it required. Every building needed a wire, and every wire needed a power supply behind it. Once that network was in place, it outgrew its first purpose almost immediately. Electric light, along with the electric elevator, allowed buildings to grow. Factories ran through the night. Cities stayed awake after dark.

Then came the unexpected uses. The first household appliances had nowhere to plug in, so people screwed fans and irons into the sockets hanging from their ceilings. In 1904, Harvey Hubbell patented a separable plug that made the connection safer and simpler. Manufacturers kept selling incompatible designs for years before settling on the parallel-blade shape that Hubbell patented, still in your wall today.

Safety rules came about the same way. According to Freeberg, insurance companies, tired of paying for electrical fires, pushed the electric companies into agreeing on the first common standards.

Once the plug was standard, anyone could build something that used it. Refrigerators, radios, washing machines, and eventually computers all came through that same wire. The light bulb may have started it, but the network built the twentieth century.

THE NETWORK IS THE PLATFORM

For more than a century, the grid’s job was to move power, while pipelines, rail lines, ports, and water systems moved physical goods. Increasingly, every one of those systems also has to move data. Every device connected to critical infrastructure, from a car charger to a data center to a pipeline valve or a rail switch, is becoming a device that sends and receives information.

AI deserves the excitement it’s getting today. But it only creates value when it can reach the equipment it’s meant to run. For utilities, pipelines, and water systems, that means the network is no longer back-office plumbing. It’s the platform every new capability will run on.

The network itself is changing. Satellites are beginning to connect directly to the devices ground networks serve, so a sensor on a pipeline far from any tower can be reached from above. The most valuable networks will work on the ground and in orbit as one, and the licensed airwaves connecting them will be among the economy’s scarcest resources.

THIS IS BIGGER THAN THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION

I realize that being bigger than the Industrial Revolution is a bold claim. The Industrial Revolution gave machines the power to do physical work. What is happening now gives machines the ability to decide and act on work as it happens, like software that spots a fault on a power line and reroutes electricity around it before customers notice. The same shift is coming to pipelines, rail lines, ports, and water systems.

It is also moving much faster. Electricity took half a century to reach most American homes. The smart meter transition took about two decades. This one will be measured in years. The network decisions infrastructure companies make now will decide which of them can take part.

WHAT THE WINNERS HAVE IN COMMON

Robert Metcalfe, who co-invented ethernet, observed that a network’s value grows with the square of the number of devices on it. Think of the fax machine: One is worthless, but each machine added makes the others more valuable. The same is true of the networks running critical infrastructure. The devices on them wear out and get replaced. A well-built network keeps carrying whatever comes next, for decades.

Nobody in 2004 was talking about AI. The utilities that built those smart grid networks are among the best positioned to use it now. Pipeline, rail, port, and water operators now face the same choice. The operators that wait will have to retrofit—tearing open the walls to run wire that should have been there from the start, and paying more for it.

And the winners plan for a network without edges, one that reaches a city substation and a remote pipeline, so they never have to bolt it on later.

HERE WE GO AGAIN

I was called crazy in 2004 for saying the grid would run on a network. I expect some people will say the same thing now when I say networks will run all the infrastructure the economy depends on.

Edison thought he was selling light. He was founding a century of infrastructure and innovation. Whoever builds the networks now, on the ground and in orbit, is founding the next.

Scott Langis president and CEO of Anterix.

#10545. Find Orphan Pages by Comparing Your Sitemap with an Internal Crawl

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A page can return 200 OK, exist in an XML sitemap, and still be practically invisible to anyone browsing the site.

You do not need a full commercial crawler to find the obvious cases. A small Node.js script can compare two things:

Anything present in the first set but missing from the second deserves investigation.

You now have URLs that the application publishes through its sitemap but that your HTML crawl could not reach.

The page might be intentionally isolated. It might exist for a campaign. Navigation might depend on JavaScript. Your crawler may have missed authentication or pagination.

Should a normal visitor reasonably be able to discover this page from another page on the site?

Google recommends using standard crawlable elements with resolvable href values for links that should be discoverable. Google's guidance on crawlable links

That is also good web architecture independent of SEO.

Internal links should not exist merely to move ranking signals around.

They should help users move between related tasks.

A technical guide might lead to a product page. A product page might link back to the configuration guide. A category page should make important child resources discoverable without requiring a user to know the exact URL.

This is why on-page SEO and internal linking are closely connected to site architecture. Good internal links clarify relationships for both visitors and crawlers.

At a broader level, crawlability is one part of technical SEO and search visibility. A page that nobody can reliably discover is difficult to evaluate regardless of how strong its content may be.

If an important URL appears disconnected because navigation is created only after client-side JavaScript runs, the script has surfaced a real architectural fact.

You can then decide whether that is acceptable.

If your application genuinely requires rendered-DOM crawling, replace the fetch-and-Cheerio layer with Playwright.

Do not make the simple crawler pretend to be something it is not.

The best output from this tool is not an "SEO score."

It is a concrete question for the development team:

This page exists. The sitemap knows about it. Why can't a normal HTML crawl reach it?

#10543. What it takes to pivot

There comes a time when many companies need to pivot. Maybe you want to expand out of your core category into a new one, or maybe you’re making a complete 180. When I joined You.com as COO in January this year, we decided to pivot by consolidating our product and business units around one core offering. Frankly, that offering had always been the heart of the company. This decision came down to evaluating three dimensions of the business: people, products, and customers.

From first-hand experience, I can tell you that how you approach a pivot’s first 90 days can make or break your business. When done ineffectively, it can leave employees and customers uncertain. When done well, you can bring both of those groups on board, united under a new vision.

Here are three tips for how to have a successful company pivot, from someone who recently navigated it.

1. ARRIVE WITH A THESIS, THEN TRY TO BREAK IT

Whether you’re coming into a company for the first time like I did, or you’re a long-time team member, you should always be evaluating its strengths and weaknesses to inform the best next steps to take. I wasn’t trying to shake things up for the sake of change. Rather, I had a series of conversations with the founder and CEO before I even stepped foot in the door that shaped my initial vision and plan for the company’s future. I developed an initial thesis for how the company should move forward. But rather than immediately implementing my ideas, I used the first 30 days to test it, finding its gaps and strengths. When exploring a pivot, keep an open mind and gauge buy-in before making any major changes.

I spent my first 30 days diving into the people, product, and customers. I took dozens of one-on-one meetings with employees from all departments and levels, spent enough hands-on time with the products to understand them, and also spoke with dozens of customers about what they liked about the products or how they would change them.

I looked at the company the way an investor would from the outside. I asked questions like: Where are we best positioned to win short-term and long-term? Where do we have true competitive advantage? Where is the best market opportunity? Where are our best win rates? Where is our biggest pipeline? Where is our best retention? Even if these answers differ from your original ideas, ego can’t change the data. These efforts validated my initial thesis and gave me the data and examples to commit to the pivot.

2. PIVOT AROUND A NORTH STAR

Teams are much more receptive in a return to the mission or reinforcement of the mission rather than a reinvention. You want to frame your pivot around a central anchor point, informed by the data. Another way to think of it is to clarify your North Star and pinpoint the business’s strengths and barriers to success.  

At You.com, we had success because like most companies, we made things that customers were willing to pay for. We also went out of our way to find solutions to specific problems they were facing. This is all positive, and in the process we made good products.

The reality was we sometimes built custom solutions for different customers which were valuable but not scalable. That’s not to say we shouldn’t have pursued it. Companies should branch out, test new ideas, and find creative solutions to new problems. Throughout this process, though, the outcome needs to serve the business’s North Star and value-creation objectives.

In our case, a pivot wasn’t completely revamping the product or service. Rather, we realized that the web search API product line was our foundation, and contributed to the majority of our revenues. However, it was not getting the majority of resources. We made the informed decision to reorient our company around this core product and went all-in.

This pivot essentially brought us home. When the company launched in 2021, we were the first to introduce LLMs in a search engine context. A year later, we were the first to connect an LLM to the web and started building the foundation for how AI uses the internet. From this, we developed easier ways for businesses to plug their AI into the web. Over time, we added different layers and custom-built different capabilities. But the pivot was to remove the layers and focus on the foundation.

If you’re facing a similar decision, go back to the people, product, and customer. If what’s working is 90% of the business, make it 100% of the business. If the energy comes from removal, and you give it an earnest shot to build the one thing you know you’re good at, watch what happens to the entire organization.

3. CREATE A SOFT LANDING FOR WHAT GETS LEFT

It’s important not to trivialize the 10% that gets removed, because those customers bought from us for a specific reason. Telling those customers we were moving on was delicate. Those relationships took years to build and I wanted them to feel honored on the way out.

Just like you found creative solutions to their original problems, continue to do that now. In our case, we spun out a joint venture with a professional services partner who could continue supporting businesses with custom-built solutions. Those customers had somewhere to go and didn’t get abandoned. And we could focus all the company resources around a core product.

Ninety days of listening and designing bought the next 90 days of full-speed work. People become aligned because you listened. The product is there because it’s what you are excited about and what you do best. The customer trusts you because you showed them focus, authenticity, and caring.

Alex Triplett is COO of You.com.

#10539. Google Voice app gets a redesign on Android, and it screams RCS [Gallery]

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a big neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”

Google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

The new look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

The most important thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent update directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

#10537. ANT update: Anthropic stock opens higher in Nasdaq debut

Update Thursday, 12:35 p.m.

Shares of Anthropic, PBC opened at $111.50 on Thursday in the year’s most hyped stock market debut. That’s roughly 34% higher than the $83 share price set before trading began—itself an increase over the AI giant’s original target range.

However, the stock quickly began to fall in the first hour and was trading at around $99 a share as of this writing.

Much of the market also moved lower, with the Nasdaq down around 0.73% as of 12:40 p.m. ET.

Original story:

Today, the most hyped IPO of the year (and that’s saying something) is expected to finally take place.

Claude LLM maker Anthropic, PBC (Nasdaq: ANT) will debut on the Nasdaq to much fanfare and lofty expectations. But while the Nasdaq opens at 9:30 a.m. ET, it’s likely Anthropic’s shares will not begin trading to the general public until later.

Here’s what you need to know.

The largest IPO in history

Today is Anthropic’s market debut, and its shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The initial public offering is the largest in history, surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June. The AI giant raised $81.3 billion in the offering.

The forthcoming stock listing is also the most-hyped of the year.

As Fast Company previously noted, Anthropic is considered a pure-play AI company. That is, the company’s sole business is artificial intelligence, as opposed to, say, SpaceX, which is mainly a space transportation and telecommunications company first, and an AI company second.

As the largest pure-play AI IPO ever, there’s a lot riding on how the shares react. If investors scoop them up and the share price pops, it could suggest that Wall Street still has an appetite for riskier AI-related stocks, despite recent pullbacks in the broader tech market.

However, don’t expect to know how ANT shares are performing as soon as the Nasdaq opens at 9:30 a.m. ET. That’s because, despite the market open, the first buy and sell orders for ANT shares likely won’t be fulfilled until later in the day.

What time do Anthropic’s shares begin trading today?

If a stock is already listed on an exchange, its shares usually begin trading to the public as soon as that exchange opens. But for market debuts, things are a little different.

Stock exchanges know that there is frequently a flurry of orders (both buy and sell) when a hot stock debuts.

If the stock were to trade immediately when the market opened, it could cause extreme price volatility, sending the stock up or down significantly in a matter of seconds. Another reason is operational: Nasdaq simply needs time to match orders—buyers with sellers—and determine a price.

Because of this, markets like the Nasdaq have procedures in place that delay trading by a little bit so buyers and sellers can get a better idea of demand and price the stock accordingly. Nasdaq calls this a Halt Cross.

Only once Nasdaq has determined an opening clearing price based on all its buy and sell orders does it release the stock for trading.

Why does this sound familiar?

If this sounds familiar, it’s because it’s exactly the same process that happened with the SpaceX IPO.

While SPCX shares debuted on the Nasdaq on June 12, they did not begin trading immediately when the Nasdaq opened at 9:30 a.m. ET. Instead, SpaceX’s shares began trading about two to three hours after the morning bell.

So, what time, then, will Anthropic’s shares actually begin trading on the Nasdaq?

It’s impossible to say for sure. Nasdaq’s rules don’t restrict the Halt Cross to a certain defined period, such as two hours. The Halt Cross lasts as long as it needs to.

However, if history is any indication, the Halt Cross usually ends anywhere from 2-4 hours after markets open.

That rough estimate suggests that Anthropic shares will begin trading at some point roughly between 11:30 a.m. ET and 1:30 p.m. ET today.

#10536. Nvidia claims its Vera CPU can gain up to 39% performance boost via software optimization at SC26 — architectural fine-tuning is needed to fully unleash custom Olympus cores

Vera can speed up old code out of the box, but there's more performance to unlock

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia's Vera CPU, designed as both a standalone data-center part and a host for Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 servers, offers impressive performance thanks to substantially higher execution resources per core than its predecessor, Grace. However, Nvidia admits at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) that existing software cannot always take full advantage of Vera's resources without adaptation for the architecture.

The company shared that architecture-specific software optimizations can boost Vera's performance by nearly 39% in certain computationally intensive workloads. But despite offering unbeatable single-thread performance, the CPU is not positioned for general-purpose workloads.

Get the full Tom's Hardware experience on your device with our brand-new app. Bookmark articles, use our smart search feature, personalize your feed, and get push notifications so you never miss a beat.

Unlike Grace, which relies on off-the-shelf Neoverse V2 CPU cores developed by Arm, Vera uses Nvidia's proprietary Olympus cores specifically designed to maximize per-core performance as well as to ensure high aggregate throughput. To that end, Nvidia equipped Olympus with a wide front end that features a 10-wide decoder, a neural branch predictor, a deep out-of-order execution engine, six vector execution units, four load pipelines, two store pipelines, all backed with large private caches and advanced prefetch mechanisms.

In fact, Nvidia deliberately opted for 88 high-performance general-purpose cores with support for its proprietary spatial multithreading technology (176 threads in total) rather than maximizing the number of cores per socket, as the maximum possible single-thread performance was one of the key design goals for Vera.

"CPU design is really just a game of trade-offs," said Hannah Coutand, who leads Vera CPU marketing at Nvidia, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium. "You could maximize for a lot of cores, but literally when you maximize the die for lots of cores, you do not actually have space to maximize for IPC, like instructions per clock."

Although Nvidia primarily positions Vera as a CPU for agentic AI and other AI-related workloads, the company originally conceived its Olympus microarchitecture with data processing applications in mind. As it turned out, the key attributes of Vera — high per-core performance, high memory bandwidth, and low memory access latency — are precisely what agentic AI workloads need as well, according to Coutand.

"We are very clear in our strategy with Vera and our positioning with Vera that it is not a general-purpose CPU," Coutand said. " If you want a web server for your cloud data center, there are probably other choices that are better suited for that than Vera. [Vera is made for] workloads […] that require that high per-core speed, high memory bandwidth, low latency. […] It has great fungibility for lots of workloads as long as those workloads value the things that Vera is good for."

To assess the computational capabilities of Nvidia's custom Olympus microarchitecture and its advantages over Neoverse V2, Nvidia's researchers used a double-precision general matrix multiplication (DGEMM) workload based on an assembly kernel from OpenBLAS, an open-source linear algebra library. While OpenBLAS features a kernel tailored for the Arm Neoverse V2 cores that power Nvidia's Grace processor, it lacks one specifically designed for Olympus.

To examine the efficiency of the two microarchitectures, the researchers used a standalone benchmark called miniKernelGEMM with a 128 × 128 matrix multiplication problem that fits into the L1 cache of both processors.

The Grace CPU achieved 4.51 instructions per clock (IPC) and 13.03 FP64 operations per cycle with the Neoverse V2 kernel, whereas Vera executed 5.43 instructions per clock and 15.69 FP64 operations per cycle with the very same code, an improvement of approximately 20%.

However, when the researchers used a kernel specifically optimized for Olympus, Vera’s performance increased to 7.53 instructions per clock and 21.75 FP64 operations per cycle. As a result, Vera outperformed its predecessor by nearly 67% on a per-core, per-clock basis in this particular workload.

Grace's Neoverse V2 microarchitecture has four 128-bit SIMD pipelines that can perform a total of 16 FP64 operations per clock, whereas Nvidia's Olympus has six such pipelines that can execute up to 24 FP64 operations per cycle, a 50% improvement.

But where the Neoverse V2-optimized kernel uses 81.4% of Grace's peak FP64 throughput, it uses only about 66.5% of Vera's computational capabilities. With changes to matrix tile organization, register allocation, and instruction scheduling that better suit the Olympus microarchitecture, the researchers managed to utilize 90.6% of its peak FP64 throughput, according to Nvidia's tutorial published at SC26.

While software developed and optimized for existing Arm-based data center processors can still benefit from the capabilities of Nvidia's Olympus cores without any specific optimizations, the company's SC26 benchmark results demonstrate that at least some applications will need to be fine-tuned for the new microarchitecture to take full advantage of its execution resources. Of course, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained through Olympus-specific optimizations in workloads other than matrix multiplication.

As Nvidia expands beyond CPUs that primarily serve as companions to its data center GPUs and chases the standalone server CPU market, the company will have to ensure that performance-critical software takes advantage of the architectural peculiarities of its processors, much like Intel and AMD have done for decades.

But the company is already deeply experienced with partner and ecosystem development for platforms like CUDA, so as Vera is more widely adopted, that experience could prove useful in spurring optimizations for these CPUs going forward.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

#10533. The real lesson businesses should learn from video games (it’s more than ‘gamification’)

In the early 2000s I (Bing) found myself crouched in an office cubicle frantically scribbling down a few things I thought the video game industry could teach a burgeoning online bookstore.

I was initially reluctant when my friend, the legendary venture capitalist John Doerr, asked me to take a meeting in Seattle with a buzzy, young startup CEO. I was a midcareer video game executive and this particular founder had already been named Time’s 1999 person of the year. Terrified to look a fool, I ducked into a cubicle at the Electronic Arts office in Seattle and outlined an idea for an online customer loyalty program based on the strategy that had turned Madden NFL into a forever franchise by giving gamers reasons to come back year after year.

I practically stuffed the one-pager in Jeff Bezos’s hand the first time we met over coffee. He laughed, but indulged me and unfurled the page. I started my career in video games as a marketing chief, and I was still in the habit of writing headline copy for all my one-pagers. Across the top of this one I wrote: Amazon Prime.

Jeff would say that Prime’s success was a good surprise, but when you know video games, when you understand the magical ways that they tap into our intrinsic motivations and make us want to come back again and again, you understand that game design thinking has the potential to increase retention and engagement in almost any walk of life. After Amazon Prime worked so well, I brought the lessons of video games to all kinds of consumer industries, from entertainment products like Spotify to financial products like Better Mortgage to educational products like Coursera and Duolingo and even weight loss apps like My Fitness Pal.

A bad rap

I used to call the craft of applying video game design to consumer products “video gamification,” but these days gamification has a bad rap. Some of the smartest business minds I know brush it off as a short-lived 2010s trend that didn’t pan out. I’ve heard countless product teams complain that the points and leaderboard systems they build into their user interfaces didn’t make a dent in any of their retention metrics. Worse still, I have friends and peers who recoil when they hear the word “gamify,” immediately assuming someone is trying to manipulate their time and attention. Gamification has taken on such a negative connotation that I’ve stopped using the word altogether.

The thing is, the so-called “gamification” trend that failed hard in the 2010s was based on a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes successful games work. Product teams that couldn’t figure out how to boost traffic to their app would probably be surprised to learn that successful games rarely rely on competition to motivate players. In fact, in video games, cooperation is a far more important mechanism than competition.

Connection, mastery, productivity

If you’re going to channel the motivational magic of a great game, you need to understand what actually goes into crafting one. The top reasons that players come back to a game are, in order of importance, social connection, personal mastery, and productivity. Most business execs I meet assume that productivity measures like money and rankings are the most important motivational forces, but the video game industry has found for decades that social relationships and the satisfaction of self-improvement far outweigh them.

In the early days of the Facebook juggernaut game Farmville, its developer, Zynga, found that the notifications that invited friends to play cooperatively garnered 30 times the clicks that the competitive, brag-based notifications did. In games, a two-way social interaction is the top predictor of whether or not somebody comes back tomorrow.

Nongamers find this surprising, but they shouldn’t! We’re human beings, ever motivated to build communities and deepen our relationships with one another. We come back to the games and products that best align with that. One of the great social features of the business networking platform Linkedin is “Endorsements,” where users are invited to publicly vouch for their peers and strengthen their professional relationships. Cooperative features like this give people a reason to return to the résumé sharing platform regularly, even when they aren’t searching for jobs.

Personal mastery and self-improvement are also intrinsic motivators to every gamer. Mechanics that give people a framework to measure and track self-improvement, like experience points and level-ups, create an invigorating sense of progress with each session. Scores are important in games, but more so as a way to rate individual progression instead of rank it against others.

Productivity measures like time saved and money earned also motivate us, especially when they’re paired with our social and mastery priorities. We like earning money, sure, but we love earning money doing things we already wanted to do, and we might forgo it when it comes in direct conflict with our social relationships and sense of self-worth.

More of what they want

Amazon Prime works because it gives its customers more of what they already want. Free and fast shipping offers an incredible productivity proposition, especially in terms of time saved, and individualized customer profiles help us form identities around ourselves as consumers. Amazon knows that one of the biggest predictors of whether a Prime user renews is how often they use their subscription benefits, but pushing members to make purchases they otherwise wouldn’t risks undermining long-term loyalty. So Amazon treats Prime like a forever game franchise, continually improving the experience and layering on new benefits like Prime Video, Amazon Music, and prescription savings. Each gives members another reason to use their subscription in ways that already align with their interests.

When I gut check a user experience to see if it’s aligned with my own wants and needs, it’s usually as simple as asking, does this product like me? Do I feel better about myself at the end of my session than I did at the beginning? If the answer is no, it usually means the designers are trying to gamify me against my own best interest, like a credit card rewards program that persuades me to spend more money than I would otherwise, or a social media platform that delivers empty dopamine hits without any meaningful upside to my social relationships.

These days, I’ve dropped the term “gamification,” but my belief in applying game thinking to products hasn’t wavered. Start with what people actually want, and build around those priorities. You’ll tap into intrinsic motivations far more powerful than any user interface trick or attention hack. That’s real video gamification, and that will always work.

#10532. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

The agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

We wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

Which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

The formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

Relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

On 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure."

Before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

The measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:

This time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

One detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a new colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

An agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and said it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

The --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

An agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer new to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

These are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

Take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

#10531. The Xiaomi 18 Pro debuts globally with sub-mm bezels, privacy display, rear display, and 200MP Leica cameras

Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC.

If you’re looking for a phone with top-tier specs, Xiaomi has a new phone for you. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are the company’s latest flagships, available starting today, November 17. When looking at the spec list for the Xiaomi 18 series, it’s difficult to find anything that was left out.

The 120Hz LTPO display is bordered by a 0.99mm bezel, the smallest in the industry so far, 4,000-nit peak brightness, and TÜV Rheinland Triple Eye Care Certification, including a 2160Hz PWM dimming rate. Inside the phone is a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor with a 3D IceLoop cooling system, and each model’s silicon-carbon battery includes 28% silicon content.

On the back is a pair of 200MP cameras, including a 1/1.28-inch main sensor and a 1/1.56-inch periscope telephoto sensor. These are massive sensors, especially compared to the 1/3.94″ and 1/2.52″ telephoto sensors in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Despite their size, Xiaomi packs them onto the back in an island with fully flat glass — no protruding camera lenses!

That island on the back isn’t just for cameras, though. It also packs in a 120Hz LTPO M11 OLED panel with 4,000-nit peak brightness for ultra-high-quality selfies and group shots, plus support for notifications and apps. Xiaomi created a new GenAI Apps feature that lets you create your own apps on the back display, plus official support for several popular apps like Google Maps, Spotify, and more.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series ships with HyperOS 4 (Android 17) and includes 3 months of Google AI Pro, plus 5TB of Google Cloud storage. The Xiaomi 18 Pro retails for €1399 for the model with 12GB RAM and 256GB storage, or €1599 for 12GB/512GB. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at €1599 for 12GB/256GB, €1799 for 12GB/512GB, and a 16GB/1TB model will be available soon for €2099.

Some retailers also sell a bundle that includes the Official silicone magnetic case, which usually retails for €39, as well as the Magnetic Remote Stand, which retails for €69. That remote stand functions as a MagSafe-style stand and remote, giving you camera shutter functionality and a scrolling feature.

#10530. No ‘credible pathway’ for the energy sector to return to the pre-Iran war days, says IEA

The world’s largest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns this year are reshaping the future of how people will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, according to an International Energy Agency report released Thursday.

The energy crisis, triggered by the Iran war, will “leave lasting marks” on the world’s energy sector, according to the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 energy crisis.

Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said. This is a boon for renewable technologies, like solar, and alternative technologies, like nuclear. But it is also reinforcing the case to keep coal as a backup in times of crisis.

This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where around a fifth of the world’s traded oil typically flows.

The report looks “past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today’s upheaval,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol. He said the Iran war “delivered a huge shock to the system” and warned “the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be.”

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” he said.

Annual United Nations climate talks, known as COP31 and hosted in Turkey this year, are in their second and final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are the two big ticket issues at this year’s climate talks.

“The future of the energy system and our climate are inextricably intertwined,” said Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at COP31.

Flagship report forecasts energy future

The IEA, the world’s leading intergovernmental energy organization with more than 30 member countries, publishes World Energy Outlooks annually.

This year’s 560-page plus report analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries will continue with current policies or drastically change policies in the face of ongoing crises.

The world’s energy sector will clearly have a before and after the Iran war, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets.

“This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “It’s crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home.”

Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures. The IEA said the “drive to diversify” fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade.

The Middle East will still be the world’s largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA forecasts the amount of oil transiting the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war, to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035.

While fossil fuels still dominate national energy mixes, the IEA said renewables — led by solar — and nuclear power are the “biggest beneficiaries” of governments trying to grow domestic energy sources. But energy security concerns may lead coal-rich nations to rely on the fossil fuel as a fallback option during times of crisis.

“When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change,” said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember.

Climate talks eye electrification

The ongoing talks in Turkey follow a year rattled by the Iran war’s energy shock, as well as several climate-induced disasters.

Global warming adds pressure to rising electricity demand. In what the IEA called a “striking milestone,” energy demand for cooling is overtaking energy demand for heating for the first time.

India, the world’s most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than any other country or region. China, already one of the world’s most electrified economies, may see its electrification grow from 32% last year to 43% by 2035 — the highest among any major economy.

At COP31, Turkey is pushing for the world to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.

While the preference would be for this to come from renewable energy, U.N. documents on the negotiating table don’t spell this out. That means coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially.

“The IEA’s latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the US-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy and electrification,” said Cleetus, with the Union of Concerned Scientists.

#10527. Instagram now lets you edit stories, but you have to act fast. Here’s how to do it

For anyone who has ever hit share, only to spot a typo moments later, Instagram now has a fix for that. The Meta-owned platform is rolling out a feature that lets you edit a story after you post it. 

Instagram head Adam Mosseri announced the new feature Wednesday in a post on his Instagram feed.

“A lot of people have been asking for this, so I’m excited to get this one out there,” he shared in the post.

You can edit text, music, stickers, and drawings, but there’s one catch: you have to act fast. You can only make edits to a story within 15 minutes of sharing.

You can fix typos and other mistakes without losing your views, likes, or replies. Previously, the only option besides leaving the story up was to delete it and repost.

A few other details worth knowing 

When you edit a story, Instagram adds an edited label, and your audience stays the same.

Any previous reshares of the story get removed. According to Instagram, editing is not available on stories that were also shared to Facebook or contain certain stickers.

How to edit an Instagram story:

  1. Open your published story.
  2. Tap the three dots “More” button.
  3. Select Edit story.
  4. Fix your text, or update stickers, drawing, or music.
  5. Save the changes.

Instagram announced the feature along with other stories upgrades, including new sticker designs, an easier way to select multiple photos, and backgrounds for photos of any size.

#10524. What does the Anthropic IPO mean for your 401(k)?

You may have no interest in investing in AI companies, and you may even suspect that the AI boom is a bubble about to pop. But you could already have a stake in one of the industry’s biggest players anyway: Anthropic, which went public today, may be in your retirement account or about to show up there.

Some mutual funds, including American Funds Growth Fund of America (AGTHX) and Fidelity Select Technology (FSPTX), hold substantial equity stakes in Anthropic. And some index funds will also soon acquire shares, after recently changing their rules to make it easier for massive companies to join shortly after going public. Previously, companies often had to wait months or a year to be included in major indexes, in part because of concerns about stock volatility.

Earlier this year, ahead of the SpaceX IPO, Nasdaq shortened its waiting period from three months to 15 trading days for qualified mega-IPOs. Nasdaq argued that companies as large as SpaceX and Anthropic shouldn’t have to wait so long.

FTSE Russell has similarly shortened its waiting period to just five trading days, though inclusion depends on how many shares are available for public trading. Morningstar already had a short five-day waiting period, but relaxed its rules about available shares. The S&P 500, meanwhile, still requires companies to wait 12 months and turn a profit before joining—two hurdles Anthropic has yet to clear.

When Anthropic is included in a retirement portfolio, it won’t have a large weight initially, Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer at Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity at Vanguard, tells Fast Company. That’s because a relatively small portion of the company’s shares will be available to public investors to begin with. Vanguard has estimated that Anthropic will represent 0.05%–0.15% of its total market index fund. If you have $500,000 in that fund, that might mean $250 to $750 worth of indirect exposure to Anthropic.

How to find Anthropic in your 401(k)

To know if your 401(k) or an index fund you own will include Anthropic, you’ll have to dig into the details. “Most people don’t look at their index funds, or anything that their 401(k) is invested in,” says John Polonis, a former Wall Street lawyer who now writes about finance. Even if you’ve chosen not to invest in the Nasdaq-100, for example, the stock could still be hiding somewhere else. Other funds, including those that invest in the largest publicly traded companies, could also hold Anthropic shares. “There may be ways that you are getting exposure,” Polonis says, “and if you don’t want any exposure at all, you really have to do a lot of diligence to kind of screen that.”

To check your own portfolio, log into your 401(k) account. If you have actively managed mutual funds, look up each fund’s portfolio holdings and search for Anthropic. If you have index funds, check to see which indexes they track. The indexes that will soon acquire Anthropic stock include Russell 1000, Russell 3000, Nasdaq-100, Morningstar U.S., FTSE Global All Cap, and MSCI USA.

Because companies like Alphabet and Amazon also own large chunks of Anthropic stock, index funds also have exposure through those companies.

The risk for passive investors is low at this point because exposure is limited. But exposure is likely to grow over time. And some critics argue that because Anthropic is still at an early stage, and not yet profitable, it shouldn’t be part of retirement accounts. Jonathan Westin, executive director of Climate Organizing Hub and part of a group called Stop Funding Billionaires that protested in front of Anthropic’s offices in advance of the IPO, argues that the company’s early investors stand to reap enormous profits while ordinary investors shoulder the risk if the AI boom collapses. “They’re all just trying to get paid out and get paid out now before the collapse,” he says. “And then the real people that are left picking up the pieces are our 401(k)s and pension funds that are going to drop.”

There’s a broader issue: major indexes are supposed to reflect the market, not shape it. But fast-tracking stocks like Anthropic arguably influences the market, says Michael Green, an investor and financial market researcher who is CEO of Tier1 Alpha Asset Management. When a new company is added to a major index and index funds automatically have to buy it, that drives up the company’s stock price. A recent study calculated that fast-tracked IPOs have a 5% price premium over those added to indexes more slowly. Index funds are stuck paying prices that are inflated by their own demand. Fast-tracked companies can also raise 6.2% more capital.

“The far more important question is whether or not is it appropriate to use a platform like an index fund to facilitate a particular class of IPO that largely serves to enrich a subset of the population on the back of a government-mandated retirement system,” Green says.

And therein lies the broader problem: Green argues that the system could give the biggest companies a disproportionate advantage over smaller competitors, reinforcing an economy increasingly dominated by big business.
